title: The gothic cathedral

cards: Stone wants to fall. Every block in a wall presses on the one below, and the higher a wall goes, the thicker its bottom has to be. Build big the plain way: heavy walls, small windows, a dim room.
Then medieval builders tried another answer. They pointed their arches, so the weight ran down more steeply. They laid ribs of stone across the ceiling to gather the load into a few strong points.
Outside, they threw arms of stone through the air, flying buttresses, to hold the walls up from beyond. Now the walls didn't carry everything. They could open up, and fill with colored glass.

teach.h: THE ROOM IS A LIFTED GAZE.
teach.b: A gothic cathedral does two things stone doesn't like to do: it rises high, and it lets light in. Some Christians have read both as more than engineering. Start with up.
Walk in, and the columns run in thin lines from floor to vault, drawing the eye upward. A psalm says, "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."
A gothic nave builds that sentence in stone: the whole room is a lifted gaze. Then, light. Much of the glass wasn't clear.
It was colored, set with scenes from the Bible, prophets, the life of Jesus, the saints, for people below to look up and see.
John's Gospel begins with light: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
On a gray morning, the light comes in already full of stories.

Third, the stones. The first letter of Peter turns the picture around and says the building is people: "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house." Lively, in the old English, means living.

So a cathedral points past itself to a congregation, each person a stone, set beside the others and holding them up. Last, the labor. These were slow buildings, raised by masons, glaziers and carpenters.

teach.h: EXCEPT THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.
teach.b: Psalm 127 puts that work in its place: "Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it." Stone, lifted toward light, and a psalm that names another builder.

how: Gothic cathedrals across Europe, and gothic-style churches built since, are still used for daily and Sunday worship; visitors and worshipers alike walk the nave, look up into the vaults, and sit beneath the stained glass.

o: a dark, heavy-walled church of thick stone
a Roman-style church with round arches and domes

s: gothic churches were built to be dark and gloomy
the whole design moves weight off the walls so they could open up and fill with colored light.
flying buttresses support the walls from outside the building
arms of stone take the outward push of the vault and carry it down to the ground outside, so the walls don't have to carry it all.
in the King James Bible, "lively stones" means living stones
1 Peter says the people themselves are "built up a spiritual house."

games.q: you're a medieval builder. you want a tall room full of light, but stone walls have to be thick to hold the roof up. what do you do?
o: make the walls thicker and the windows smaller
carry the weight outside with stone arms, and fill the walls with glass
games.why: gothic builders pointed their arches, ribbed their ceilings and propped the walls from outside, so the walls could become windows.

practice: Wherever you are, a church, a stairwell, or just under your own ceiling, let your eyes start at the floor and climb slowly, the way the eye climbs a column, to the highest point you can see, and rest them there.
If you pray, say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. If not, just keep your eyes up.

wordCard.voice: The gothic cathedral. A church built in stone that lifts the weight off its walls, so it can rise high and fill with colored light.

orig.note: Greek: living stones, from 1 Peter 2:5, which the King James renders "lively stones."

carryVoice: Your line: stone reaching up. Heavy things, lifted into light. Same time tomorrow.
